observation: A controlled study found simple letter-spacing manipulation improved reading speed >20% and halved errors in dyslexic children, same-day, attributed to reduced visual crowding rather than font family; a follow-up found spacing (not 'dyslexia-friendly' fonts) drove the readability gain, with very tight or very wide line spacing both hurting and ~1.5x line spacing as a reasonable default.
claim: Letter/word/line spacing (not font family) is a cheap, evidence-backed, high-leverage typography setting that helps dyslexic readers with an immediate, no-training effect — distinct from the debunked dyslexia-font claim.
mechanism: Spacing manipulation reduces visual crowding between adjacent letters/words, a distinct mechanism from font shape.
population: children with dyslexia; population is dyslexic readers, not Sam

implications.text: Offer letter/word/line spacing and shorter line length as an explicit typography setting (not a 'dyslexia font' feature, which is debunked), default to ~1.5x line height.

observation: Monotropism theory (Murray, Lesser & Lawson 2005, developed by autistic researchers) reframes autistic attention as concentrated on few interests at once; the primary source states task-switching is exceptionally demanding, describing an unanticipated interruption as 'truly, if briefly, catastrophic.'
claim: Interruption design must distinguish ADHD's 'attention drifts and needs re-anchoring' from autism's 'forced task-switch is acutely costly' — these need different, possibly opposite, interruption defaults, not one population-wide policy.
mechanism: Monotropic attention is deeply focused on few interests, so forced redirection from a well-functioning focus state is qualitatively more costly than the wandering-attention pattern ADHD research describes.
population: autistic adults; lived-experience theoretical framework from autistic scholars, not an RCT-backed causal model

implications.text: Any future interruption/notification feature should default to not interrupting an active session at all, and warn before switching context if it must, rather than switching abruptly — a stricter constraint than ADHD-only research implies.

observation: ME/CFS and long COVID pacing guidance (NICE 2021 guideline, WHO-endorsed) treats cognitive effort as a depletable, slowly-replenishing resource where overuse causes delayed, multi-day crashes (post-exertional symptom exacerbation), not an in-session lapse; the brain uses ~20% of body energy on ~2% of body mass, a profound vulnerability for this population.
claim: A capacity model built around ADHD's spiky, same-session fluctuation will misread ME/CFS/long-COVID needs — this population needs a budget that persists and rolls over across sessions/days, and 'I have capacity right now' can be actively misleading since the crash arrives later.
mechanism: Post-exertional symptom exacerbation is delayed by hours to days, so feeling fine while reading is not proof the reading stayed within budget.
population: adults with ME/CFS or long COVID; population is not Sam (ADHD)

implications.text: If Riemann generalizes its capacity dial beyond Sam, add a retrospective/predictive layer ('how did yesterday's reading load feel today'), not just a per-session 'how much can you take on right now' slider.

observation: A 2025 study comparing original, human-simplified, and AI-simplified text for L2 readers found neither simplified version was significantly easier to comprehend than the original once the reader's topic familiarity was statistically controlled, suggesting apparent 'simplification helps' effects in less-controlled studies may really be a familiarity/vocabulary-coverage effect.
claim: Riemann's core premise that L0/L1 abstraction levels aid comprehension should be treated as an empirically testable hypothesis, not a given — this directly challenges the implicit assumption that compression itself does the comprehension work.
mechanism: Once topic familiarity is controlled for, the apparent benefit of text simplification for L2 comprehension largely disappears, implying familiarity rather than syntactic simplicity may be doing the work in less-controlled prior studies.
population: non-native (L2) English readers; population is L2 learners, not Sam
context: well-controlled 2025 study, directly on AI-generated simplification

implications.text: Instrument Riemann to test whether the abstraction tree's comprehension gain is real for Sam specifically (opt-in comprehension spot-checks comparing L0/L1-only vs. L3 engagement), rather than assuming compression itself helps.

observation: A 2026 systematic review of Easy Read materials found real-world Easy Read content often has actual reading ages of 13-14 years, far above the ~8-year-old target the guidance claims to hit, and found no study showing statistically significant comprehension or behavior-change gains attributable to Easy Read formatting itself; common guideline elements (short sentences, bullets, images) are widely prescribed but largely untested individually.
claim: 'Easy Read'-style simplification guidelines should not be adopted as a confident, checkbox feature — the evidence for individual guideline components is weak, mirroring the caution already flagged for unverified 'bullet points reduce load' claims.
mechanism: A systematic review found an absence of evidence for the guideline's own components, not merely thin evidence — the format has spread through policy adoption faster than validation.
population: people with intellectual disabilities; population is not Sam

implications.text: Do not adopt Easy Read guideline elements as a confident built-in simplification feature without original usability testing against that population.

observation: WCAG 4.1.3 (Status Messages, AA) requires level changes to be programmatically announceable; ARIA live-region best practice specifies aria-live='polite' (not 'assertive') for routine user-initiated changes, aria-atomic='true' so the whole announcement is read, and a persistent empty live region populated via script rather than a freshly-injected toast, which commonly fails silently in real screen readers.
claim: Zoom-level change announcements must use a persistent, script-populated aria-live='polite' + aria-atomic='true' region, not a naive injected toast, to avoid a well-known silent-failure pattern in real assistive technology.
mechanism: A freshly-injected DOM element is a known gotcha that frequently fails silent-AT pickup despite looking correct in code review; the persistent-region pattern is the validated workaround.
context: normative WCAG standard plus converging practitioner implementation guidance

implications.text: Implement level-change announcements as a persistent, empty-at-load, script-populated aria-live='polite'/aria-atomic='true' region, not a freshly-injected toast.

observation: A slider-style continuous dial is not natively screen-reader-operable unless implemented as role='slider' with aria-valuemin/max/now/valuetext and full keyboard support; aria-valuetext should carry the human-readable level label ('Level 1 of 4: summary'), not just numeric position, since raw position is meaningless for an abstraction tree.
claim: The zoom dial needs two synchronized representations from day one: a visual slider for sighted/pointer users, and a discrete, headed/landmarked navigable document structure for screen-reader users — not one faked as the other.
mechanism: A visual analog slider has no meaning to a non-visual user unless exposed as a proper ARIA form control with a semantically meaningful valuetext, and screen-reader users navigate via keyboard/semantic structure, not pointer gestures.
population: low-vision and screen-reader users; not Sam-specific
context: assistive-technology vendor/practitioner sources, WAI-ARIA authoring practice

implications.text: Implement role='slider' with full keyboard operation and aria-valuetext level labels, plus expose each abstraction level as a landmark/heading-navigable region as a redundant native AT interaction path.

observation: The curb-cut effect (originating from literal wheelchair curb cuts later used by strollers, luggage, bikes) has well-documented digital analogs — captioning, screen-reader-driven structure, and simplified/plain-language content all get used far beyond their original target population; W3C COGA's own scope already spans ADHD, dyslexia, autism, memory impairment, anxiety, and age-related decline under one framework.
claim: Riemann should default to one accessible, low-extraneous-load substrate for everyone (plain sentences, consistent structure, chunking, low memory demand, user-paced advancement, always-available help), not ten different population-specific UIs.
mechanism: Accessible defaults built for one group are repeatedly observed to benefit far more people than the original target population once shipped broadly.
population: general population; the curb-cut effect is by definition cross-population

implications.text: Treat universal low-load defaults (plain sentences, consistent structure, chunking, low memory demand, always-visible help) as Riemann's baseline for every user, with personalization as adjustable settings layered on top.
